CHAPTER 6
 
Jos 6:1-7. Jericho Shut Up.

1. Now Jericho was straitly shut up--This verse is a parenthesis introduced to prepare the way for the directions given by the Captain of the Lord's host.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2018"/><div sID="gen2690" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2018"/><hi type="bold">3-5. ye shall compass the city, all ye men of war. ... Thus shalt thou do six days, &c.--</hi>Directions are here given as to the mode of procedure. Hebrew, "horns of jubilee"; that is, the bent or crooked trumpets with which the jubilee was proclaimed. It is probable that the horns of this animal were used at first; and that afterwards, when metallic trumpets were introduced, the primitive name, as well as form of them, was traditionally continued. The design of this whole proceeding was obviously to impress the Canaanites with a sense of the divine omnipotence, to teach the Israelites a memorable lesson of faith and confidence in God's promises, and to inspire sentiments of respect and reverence for the ark as the symbol of His presence. The length of time during which those circuits were made tended the more intensely to arrest the attention, and to deepen the impressions, both of the Israelites and the enemy. The number seven was among the Israelites the symbolic seal of the covenant between God and their nation [Keil, Hengstenberg]. <div eID="gen2690" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2020"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Josh.6.8-Josh.6.19">Jos 6:8-19</reference>. The City Compassed Six Days.</title> <div sID="gen2692" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2020"/><hi type="bold">8-11. the seven priests bearing the seven trumpets ... passed on before the Lord--</hi>before the ark, called "the ark of the covenant," for it contained the tables on which the covenant was inscribed. The procession was made in deep and solemn silence, conforming to the instructions given to the people by their leader at the outset, that they were to refrain from all acclamation and noise of any kind until he should give them a signal. It must have been a strange sight; no mound was raised, no sword drawn, no engine planted, no pioneers undermining--here were armed men, but no stroke given; they must walk and not fight. Doubtless the people of Jericho made themselves merry with the spectacle [Bishop Hall]. <div eID="gen2692" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2024"/><div sID="gen2696" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2024"/><hi type="bold">17-19. And the city shall be accursed--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Lev.27.28">Le 27:28</reference>). The cherem, or "anathema," was a devotion to utter destruction (<reference osisRef="Deut.7.2">De 7:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.20.17">20:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.3">1Sa 15:3</reference>). When such a ban was pronounced against a hostile city, the men and animals were killed--no booty was allowed to be taken. The idols and all the precious ornaments on them were to be burned (<reference osisRef="Deut.7.25">De 7:25</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Chr.14.12">1Ch 14:12</reference>). Everything was either to be destroyed or consecrated to the sanctuary. Joshua pronounced this ban on Jericho, a great and wealthy city, evidently by divine direction. The severity of the doom, accordant with the requirements of a law which was holy, just, and good, was justified, not only by the fact of its inhabitants being part of a race who had filled up their iniquities, but by their resisting the light of the recent astonishing miracle at the Jordan. Besides, as Jericho seems to have been defended by reinforcements from all the country (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.11">Jos 24:11</reference>), its destruction would paralyze all the rest of the devoted people, and thus tend to facilitate the conquest of the land; showing, as so astounding a military miracle did, that it was done, not by man, but by the power and through the anger, of God. <div eID="gen2696" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2026"/><div sID="gen2699" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2026"/><hi type="bold">20-21. So the people shouted when the priests blew with the trumpets--</hi>Towards the close of the seventh circuit, the signal was given by Joshua, and on the Israelites' raising their loud war cry, the walls fell down, doubtless burying multitudes of the inhabitants in the ruins, while the besiegers, rushing in, consigned everything animate and inanimate to indiscriminate destruction (<reference osisRef="Deut.20.16">De 20:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.20.17">17</reference>). Jewish writers mention it as an immemorial tradition that the city fell on the Sabbath. It should be remembered that the Canaanites were incorrigible idolaters, addicted to the most horrible vices, and that the righteous judgment of God might sweep them away by the sword, as well as by famine or pestilence. There was mercy mingled with judgment in employing the sword as the instrument of punishing the guilty Canaanites, for while it was directed against one place, time was afforded for others to repent. <div eID="gen2699" type="x-p"/>
